newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk Institute sees Polish '97 GDP of 5.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk Institute sees Polish '97 GDP of 5.4 pct.

text.p: Poland's 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to slow to 5.4 percent from an estimated 5.6 percent in 1996 and seven percent in 1995, according to the independent think tank Gdansk Institute.
The think tank also said on Thursday it expected GDP to further slow to 4.8 percent in 1998.

The private institute for Market Economy Research (IBnGR) also said December 1997 year-on-year inflation was likely to ease to 15 to 16 percent, rather than to the government's forecast of 13 percent forecast. That drop would be from 18.5 percent inflation in December 1996.

Gdansk said it expected a higher rate of inflation than the government mainly because domestic consumption, seen in the 40-percent boom of credit for the non-financial sector last year, was growing quicker than GDP.

"Last year was good for the Polish economy but not good enough to create foundations for a big leap forward, which Poland needs to catch up with Western Europe," IBnGR president Janusz Dabrowski told a news conference.
"We will see a stabilisation of economic indices in the coming years," he said.
Dabrowski expected 1997 growth to continue being fuelled by domestic demand and investment, despite an expected easing in these two areas from last year's nine and 18.7 percent, respectively.
Last year, demand and investment replaced exports expansion as the main catalyst for Poland's economic growth.
In 1996, exports growth declined to 6.1 percent from 18.4 percent in 1995. Imports imports grew 20.1 percent against 22.7 percent in 1995.

The drop in exports growth was a result of weak economic performance in Western countries and of zloty appreciation. The central bank allowed the zloty to rise to contain the 1995 inflationary boom from currency reverves, Dabrowski said.
Slower exports growth led to a widening trade deficit to more than $8 billion last year from nearly $2 billion in 1995.

IBnGR's analyst Miroslaw Gronicki said though the economic recovery in the West should lift Poland's exports next year, the trade gap was still likely to rise to $14 billion in 1997 and to $15.3 billion in 1998.
He said the ballooning trade gap would no longer be sufficiently offset by cross-border retail trade, which brings in about $6 billion annually, and foreign investment inflows.
The higher deficit may gradually cut currency reserves, which would pressure the zloty and undermine anti-inflationary policies, he said.
But "the zloty is unlikely to stay strong considering the worsening of the deficit," Granicki said. He added the dollar was likely to cost about 3.35-3.4 zlotys at the end of 1997.

He also said that meeting the 13-percent inflation target in 1997 would require much smaller than planned wage increases, especially for pensioners and public workers, which was unlikely in the year of parliamentary elections.
On the other hand, the expected high agricultural output in 1997 would help fight inflation, he said.
